did_you_know.text: Psalm 31 opens with the heading “For the director of music. A psalm of David,” indicating that it was intended for the director of music and attributed to David, according to the heading.
At the very beginning of the psalm, the request for deliverance is based on God’s righteousness: “Rescue me in your righteousness.” The psalmist asks God to act to save him.
The psalmist uses several successive images of protection: a rock, a stronghold, a fortified house, a boulder, and a fortress. These images emphasize the sense of security he seeks in God.

In the verse “Into your hands I commit my spirit,” the psalmist expresses the complete entrusting of his life to God’s care, and concludes with the declaration, “You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth.”
The psalm contrasts “worthless idols” with trust in God: the psalmist rejects reliance on things of no value and declares, “But I trust in the Lord.”

The psalmist acknowledges that God has seen his affliction and known the troubles of his soul. He also describes salvation as a move from confinement into open space: “You have set my feet in a spacious place.”

At the center of the psalm, suffering is described as encompassing the whole person: “my eyes,” “my soul and body.” The description combines physical and emotional distress, not merely external danger.
The distress also appears as social isolation: the psalmist describes himself as a disgrace to his enemies, a source of fear to his acquaintances, and someone whom people see and then flee from.
The statement “My times are in your hands” expresses faith that the psalmist’s life and its seasons are in God’s hands. He follows it with a request to be rescued from his enemies and persecutors.
At the end of the psalm, the appeal becomes universal: not only the psalmist, but all God’s faithful people are called to love the Lord, be strong, and take courage as they hope in him.
